counterexample: Step 0029 asserts: for the assignment A[A[0]-1] := A[0] under the precondition A[0] = 2 AND A[1] = 3, the "correct postcondition" is A[0] = 1 AND A[1] = 1. Concrete trace refuting this. The precondition pins the (relevant part of the) state uniquely, so take the array A = [2, 3], i.e. A[0] = 2, A[1] = 3 (length(A) = 2). Execute A[A[0]-1] := A[0]: (i) evaluate the index expression A[0]-1 = 2-1 = 1; (ii) evaluate the right-hand side A[0] = 2; (iii) store: A[1] := 2. Final state: A = [2, 2], i.e. A[0] = 2 and A[1] = 2. The claimed postcondition fails on its very first conjunct, since A[0] = 2 != 1 (and A[1] = 2 != 1). Because the precondition determines the post-state uniquely and execution is deterministic and error-free (index 1 is in bounds), the Hoare triple {A[0] = 2 AND A[1] = 3} A[A[0]-1] := A[0] {A[0] = 1 AND A[1] = 1} is false under both partial and total correctness -- it is not merely unprovable by simple substitution. The correct postcondition is A[0] = 2 AND A[1] = 2. Equivalently, using the array-update substitution A <- A[i <- E] that the step itself recommends: with i = A[0]-1 = 1 and E = A[0] = 2, the updated array is A[1 <- 2] = [2, 2], again contradicting A[0] = 1 AND A[1] = 1. (Sanity check that no reading rescues the claim: writing value A[0]-1 = 1 instead would give A = [2,1], and index A[0] = 2 would be out of bounds; no reading yields [1,1].)
reasoning_summary: Verified in order. Steps 0001-0003: the observation that the questioner's rule is not an axiom but a rule needing well-formedness hypotheses, and that side-effect-free expressions need only preconditions, is correct. Steps 0004-0011: the wf judgments are coherent -- {P} E wf entails {P AND 0 <= E < length(A)} A[E] wf (strengthening the precondition with the bounds obligation), and the additive rule propagates P to both operands. Steps 0012-0015: the assignment rule {P[x<-E]} E wf / {P[x<-E]} x := E {P} correctly conjoins the standard backward assignment axiom with the expression's well-formedness obligation discharged under the precondition. Step 0017: the alternative 'error value plus Error predicate' design is coherent, as are the two rules at 0018-0024 -- the unconditional one weakens the postcondition to P OR Error, and the conditional one discharges P[x<-E] => E does not evaluate to error to recover P. Step 0027: treating run-time errors as nontermination is a legitimate (if evasive) partial-correctness reading. Step 0029 is where verification fails. Its general point (naive textual substitution P[A[i]<-E] is unsound for compound variables, e.g. IsSorted(A) contains no occurrence of A[i] and so is left unchanged, and one must substitute on the array itself, A <- A[i<-E]) is right, but the concrete illustration is arithmetically false: it states that A[A[0]-1] := A[0] under A[0]=2 AND A[1]=3 has correct postcondition A[0]=1 AND A[1]=1, whereas the actual (unique, deterministic, in-bounds) result is A[0]=2 AND A[1]=2. The step thus asserts a false Hoare triple as the target the substitution rule is supposed to reproduce, which also undermines the illustration itself -- the real difficulty being illustrated (needing to evaluate A[0] to resolve the index) is misreported. Minor additional defect in the same step: 'the assignment A[i] <- P might invalidate P' should read A[i] <- E; P is a predicate, not an expression. Stopped at 0029 with the witness above.
